Hi there, I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Dr. Carter—I’m a clinician who specializes in the emotional well-being of new moms. Today we’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s a simple 10-question check-in that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling in the past week so we can be sure you’re getting the support you deserve. Everything you share stays between us, and there’s no right or wrong answer—just whatever feels true for you. When you’re ready, I’ll ask the questions one at a time. Let’s start:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?
Sometimes I can still laugh—like when my husband sends me those silly memes—but it feels a little forced. I don’t find things as funny as I used to, and it takes more effort to smile.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, that’s pretty much how it is for me—most of the time I can still laugh, but it’s not as easy or as often as before the baby.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I still look forward to some stuff—like my mom coming over or my favorite show—but the excitement feels kind of muted, like I’m going through the motions more than really feeling it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Yesterday the baby was fussy for hours and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that upset her, or that I’m just not soothing her right. I know it’s probably not my fault, but the thought still pops in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll suddenly feel my heart racing while she’s napping—like, what if she stops breathing and I don’t notice? The worry hits out of nowhere, but I can usually tell myself she’s fine and it fades after a minute or two.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky, more like a quick jolt of “what-if” that passes. It’s not an all-out scared feeling—just those little surges of worry that come and go.
Things have been getting on top of me
Some days, yeah. When she won’t nap and the laundry’s piled up, I feel like I’m drowning a little, but I tell myself to tackle one thing at a time and I manage. It’s stressful, but not hopeless.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, I wouldn’t say I’m that unhappy. I do have nights where I lie awake replaying the day—wondering if I did enough or if she ate enough—but it’s more restless thoughts than being so upset I can’t sleep.
I have felt sad or miserable
I get little waves of sadness, mostly in the evenings when I’m tired. It’s not constant—maybe a couple of times this week—but it lingers for an hour or so and then lifts.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried twice this week—once when she wouldn’t latch and once when my partner found me folding onesies at 2 a.m. It wasn’t an all-day thing; the tears just came, I let them out, and then I felt a bit better.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’ve felt tired and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 13: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Date: [today]

Symptoms endorsed  
– Reduced ability to experience pleasure/humor (Q1, Q2)  
– Self-blame/guilt over infant care (Q3)  
– Episodic, intrusive “what-if” worries about infant safety; mild physiologic arousal, no frank panic (Q4, Q5)  
– Periodic feelings of being overwhelmed; manageable with effort (Q6)  
– Evening waves of sadness, twice-weekly tearfulness (Q8, Q9)  
– Sleep-onset delay due to ruminating, not severe insomnia (Q7)  

Risk profile  
Depressive features: mild–moderate (pleasure reduction, guilt, intermittent tearfulness).  
Anxiety features: sub-clinical but notable (brief heart-racing episodes, safety worries).  
No anhedonia global or pervasive; no self-harm ideation; no suicidal thoughts.  

Screening impression  
Findings suggest subsyndromal postpartum mood distress with mixed depressive/anxiety features; current safety risk low. Continue monitoring; consider formal assessment (PHQ-9/EPDS, GAD-7) and follow-up within 1–2 weeks to evaluate trajectory.
